records.title: Show HN: Musql, JIT-compiled SQL, up to 300x faster than SQLite, 1000x vs. Turso
records.author: dsamy
records.storyText:
Howdy HN!

Missing a fast pure Go embedded SQL database. The issue is that compared to C, go is slow. Having done a lot of JIT in go, I naturally wanted to stick a JIT that generates native query kernels and see what happens.

Result: musql. Pronounced "muscle."

On a 100K-row filtered count, musql takes 21 µs: about 300x faster than C SQLite and nearly 1,000x faster than Turso. Single-threaded, warm cache, using musql's direct API, native C SQLite, and Turso's Go driver. Filtered sums are 130x faster than C SQLite, grouped aggregates 95x.

It works with Go's database/sql or through a server for libSQL clients. It uses its own storage format, with SQLite import/export. And yes, the SQL VM runs DOOM.

Code, setup, and benchmarks: https://github.com/samyfodil/musql

records.title: Show HN: I improvised my own programming language from scratch
records.author: themondayguy
records.storyText:
I always wanted to create my own programming language. Sometimes, when I was bored, I would open my computer and start improvising one (in C# on OnlineGDB, because Visual Studio is so heavy and I only open it for serious projects), but I always abandoned it after a few minutes when I realized I didn't even know how to begin.

I didn't want to follow a tutorial or anything. I wanted to figure it out myself. I didn't know what a parser was, what a lexer was, what a syntax tree was, or even what an interpreter was. My mindset was basically: "I want to write a program that gets a string containing code and does what it says."

But one of those times when I was bored, I tried again, and things just started to click. I'm not sure why it worked this time, but I succeeded in making SOMETHING.

I wrote a little program that allowed me to set and print variables, and from then on (it's been a year now), I just kept improving it.

At one point, I had previously written some code for coloring C# code (red strings, green comments, purple numbers...), so I just copy-pasted it into my new language project and hop - I had a lexer.

Basically, the way it works is that I have `interface IOperation { void Make(); }` and `interface IReadingOperation { IValue Read(); }`, and every statement or expression gets parsed into an instance of one of these interfaces.

For example, I have `class VariableDeclarationOperation(Variable v, IValue initVal) : IOperation {...}`, and when the user writes `var a = 0`, it gets parsed into an instance of this `VariableDeclarationOperation` class. Then I just iterate over these instances and execute them.

Now it really looks like a real language. I use it as the scripting language for my game engine, and it's actually running simple games! It has functions, classes, attributes... and everything uses my own syntax and all.

So yeah, I discover weird bugs all the time, but it works well enough to power some cool arcade games. And I've done A LOT of performance work to get it to this point.

Everything is fully open source!

Just wanted to share it here :)

records.title: Show HN: Zero dependency cross-language background job queue server
records.author: d11wtq
records.storyText:
I'm Chris, and this is Zizq, a centralised job queue with a heap of awesome features I won't list off here.

https://github.com/zizq-labs/zizq

It gets through the queue fast under heavy throughput and requires no setup out of the box. The server is built in Rust as a single static binary, and it provides its own durable storage via an LSM tree storage engine (fjall), and aims to make searching and mutability of jobs first-class considerations. For example you can update jobs that are sitting in the middle of a queue without draining them and re-queueing them.

The server interacts with clients through a HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 API, using a persistent streaming connection with heartbeats and automated CI-tested disconnect or network partition/split detection, which acts as the liveness probe on both client and server. Because it's HTTP, clients are easy to write without re-inventing the queue machinery. Do it with curl and shell scripts on the command line if you really want to (I've actually done this but that is not released as I would strongly advise against doing such a thing in production). As of now there are four official clients, for Node, Rust, Elixir and Ruby. More to follow in due course and/or on request.

Jobs are always written to the LSM tree to ensure durability, but LSM trees are well optimised for write-heavy workloads like job queues (they always write sequentially) and internally Zizq employs some techniques like write coalescing and some lightweight use of in-memory skip list structures to get the most bang for buck out of the LSM tree storage.

Feedback and questions appreciated.

records.title: Show HN: HieraticBench – Can AI read ancient Egyptian handwriting?
records.author: amoursy
records.storyText:
I'm obsessed with Egyptology. During covid, I wanted to get a hieratic tattoo. For those who don't know, hieratic is the cursive form of hieroglyphs that was used in day-to-day life in ancient Egypt. It's as old as hieroglyphs.

I then went on a mission to have a sentence translated into hieratic. Luckily, in 2022, I was able to commission an Oxford Egyptologist to write it for me. After that, I took it to a hieratic specialist I found on Instagram to redraw it with "biblical" accuracy.

When generative AI came out, I realized that models very rarely identify hieratic and almost never translate it correctly. Every single time a new model came out, I ended up testing my sentence and hieratic texts in general, and I realized this could actually become a benchmark. Since so many benchmarks are becoming saturated, we need to find weird ways to test new models.

That's why I decided to build HieraticBench.

The first version of the benchmark has 268 items, including real documents, signs, and other Egyptian scripts, which I used as controls, as well as my unpublished sentence in two different renditions. The current state-of-the-art foundation models are hilariously bad at identifying my sentence, especially the one the Egyptologist wrote with her pen. Some of them said Tibetan, Urdu, Korean, and, funnily enough, "Reformed Egyptian," which is from the Book of Mormon.

On real documents, the best model in the benchmark identified hieratic correctly 95% of the time, and the best score for reading individual signs was around 13%. That's when we tell the model specifically that it's hieratic. None of them can really translate a sealed sentence that's never been published and has no answer key.

I haven't run every model on every task just to keep costs down. My next steps were to run Astra and Gemini 3.1 Pro on real documents. Currently, only the Claude models have done the sign readings.

And just FYI, I have no experience whatsoever running benchmarks or evaluations, so not 100% sure I scored things right.

Things we need: - Running the models I haven't covered - More sealed sentences and labeled signs

If you know hieratic or have an Egyptologist friend, reach out at hieraticbench@veeza.ai.

Source code: https://github.com/alymoursy/hieraticbench

I'll be around to answer questions.

records.title: Show HN: Chelis, a tensor language agents can write and prove
records.author: jeffreysmith
records.storyText:
We just open sourced Chelis, a programming language we built focused on agent authorship and human supervision. You can find a longer intro on our site: https://chelis.ch/blog/launch/ But here are the key things a HN reader might like to know:

* Statically typed, compiled, functional language, with heavy influences from ML family languages

* Built for agent authorship of programs across the compiler, MCP, skills, and remdiation paths

* Formal methods baked in via SMT and related solvers being connected with the type system in the compiler

* Rich support for numerical programs and mathematically rich domains like quant finance and quant econ

* GPU support is in an experimental state, for folks who want to build from source and run on AMD or Apple acceleration

* All built in Rust

From our experience, agents can already write Chelis as well as they can write Python. And they are a lot less overconfident in incorrect approaches with all the help Chelis provides.

Several of us on the core team are hanging out on HN. Drop us a comment if you check out the work.

records.author: chancelloradams
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm sharing a game I've been building for the last few months.

You run a tech company, starting with a few engineers and a Monolith. Requirements earn revenue, revenue unlocks funding, and funding hires more engineers. Let tech debt pile up or morale slide, and your engineers get less done, or quit. Once someone IPOs, a clock starts and the highest valuation wins. Or you can win the AI Race.

I've been an engineer in tech for a long time. I was aiming for something that allowed me to visually represent a software stack like you see or build at modern tech companies. I also wanted something tongue-in-cheek about the silly things we say (YAGNI, KISS) and the shitty things that happen at companies (layoffs, audits), but deep enough for real strategy. Inspired by some of my faves: Lichess, MTG, Twilight Struggle, Slay the Spire, Balatro.

You can play a tutorial, a bot, pass-and-play, or the online arena: ranked matches or private rooms with friends. You can also create an account and connect agents which play in their own lane over MCP. Pipe dream: Monolith becomes a new benchmark for AI releases.

Tech stack: TypeScript/Node (for now; rust rewrite of the engine is on the table...). Matches stream over server-sent events, and the same rules engine runs the server and the bots.

Feedback is much appreciated, here or via Report a bug in the menu. I'm especially curious whether the first few turns make sense.

records.title: Show HN: PanelAlpha Engine – Turn your VPS into a programmable hosting layer
records.author: konradkeck
records.storyText:
PanelAlpha Engine is an open-source hosting environment for your VPS, programmable through MCP, API and CLI.

After ~2 years in the making (we started back in the non-ai era) we've decided to open source our Docker-based Engine. So far, we've used it as a back-end environment for WordPress sites and we have been distributing it through web hosting providers and larger agencies. It's been tested on a few thousand sites already.

Now people are vibe coding, using AI for everything and building agentic workflows, while at the same time open source projects are getting through a reinassaince. So, not only we have open-sourced it ourselves, but we've also expanded it to support any web application and tested it against over a thousand repositories (and soon will be much more).

You can use it with MCP, API or CLI to: - deploy projects from files or git - get a preview URL or use your own domain with automatic SSL - restrict access with a password - get built-in monitoring and visitor stats (no need for Google Analytics) - manage databases, SFTP/FTP, CRON, firewall rules - read through logs and debug - create or restore backups (locally or remotely via S3/FTP) - connect with Cloudflare (for tunnels and DNS) ... and much more (see docs).

You install it with one command (you can also define a repo to be installed together with it) and then with another command connect your AI with it. Done. Your agent gets a hosting environment on your server without unrestricted root SSH access. You can even define its permissions.

Our early users have asked us about the visual/panel - it will be available soon too (and also open source).

Feel free to roast, we're open for feedback!

records.storyText:
A friend and I built this for our own calls and are sharing it as is. The itch: we kept copy-pasting Granola transcripts into Claude mid-call, and wondered what would happen if the agent just joined.

Two-minute demo: https://youtu.be/XhCSRiiL67A

How it works: a local Electron app joins the Meet in its own browser as a participant. Your agent drives it over MCP (or HTTP): tools to listen, speak, and write to a shared whiteboard. Any MCP agent works; we built for Claude Code first, and Codex and Cursor run it too. It is your actual session, on your machine, in your repo, with your skills, so it can do real work during the call instead of summarizing afterwards.

The hack: by default it does no speech recognition of its own. It reads Meet's live captions, and speaks through a virtual microphone. This is cheap and surprisingly good! (There is also an experimental realtime mode in app preferences that puts OpenAI's speech-to-speech model in the voice seat, with your agent feeding it facts.)

Bring an ElevenLabs key for a better voice. Works with Google Meet and Slack huddles today; Zoom is in progress. Known issues are in the README.

Try it in your next Google Meet and surprise a friend. Let us know what you think!

I built Keel because writing one-off scripts with AI or putting LLMs in the execution loop is not reliable, slow and hard to audit. You end up with lots of subtle errors with time series data.

records.author: ravikapoor101
records.storyText:
Author here. Bees is an agentic harness that runs on your own machine — macOS, Windows and Linux, MIT/Apache 2.0.

The problem we kept hitting in client work: every agent platform wanted to be the place your documents live. We wanted the opposite — the orchestrator reads your files in place, on your disk, and we never see them.

How it works: you describe work in plain English, Bees proposes the agents, stages, tools and schedule, and nothing runs until you apply it. Agents execute locally in their own run folders. A separate reviewer agent checks output before it advances a stage. Agents stop and ask for approval before external side effects like sending mail.

Coordination is deliberately thin. In a Regular org we sync team membership, process runs and stages, work claims, and file names with relative paths. Not contents. If you want no third party at all, pick a local model and local tools and it runs fully offline.

Model routing is BYO: local models, your own API keys, or the official Claude Code CLI you already have installed and signed into as yourself. We don't intermediate credentials and we add no per-token or per-run fee — that's the whole point.

Rough edges, honestly: {name the two weakest things — I'd lead with whatever your beta testers actually complained about}. Scripted installers exist but Linux distro coverage is the thinnest. Very happy to answer architecture questions, and I'd particularly like pushback from anyone running multi-machine setups.

records.author: Liebmann5
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Nick. I'm a self-taught programmer with some B.S. in Applied Math, currently working construction but for the past few years have been building something that I think is extremely cool which is AA! My goal was to create a tool to hopefully help folks get jobs, and in the process perhaps gather and showcase job market data from a different perspective that I believe contains stories, ideas, and considerations worthy of sharing.

As of right now, AA has never successfully submitted anything, but I'm hoping that will all change very soon. Worst-case scenario users were my target audience with the goal being have it run efficiently, accurately, and reliably! I figured, if I could achieve something capable of functioning in this way then that would mean maximum availability to those who need it most.

- Customization Central Tons of ways to run: clone it, from a Flashdrive, inside Docker? Perhaps you only want it to collect qualified/aligned links or have it just apply to the links you provide or even Human in the Loop with set checkpoints? Avoid LinkedIn and Indeed and other login required sites, no problem!

- Download AA to a flash drive and plug it into a local library computer. I got the opportunity to work with my local library to offer folks sessions where they get AA up and running and while it does its thing they go and learn useful job skills and practice.

- Autonomy through Geometry: no hardcoded selectors anywhere. AA reads pages geometrically instead: Kuhn–Munkres assignment to optimally pair form labels to their inputs, convex hulls and VIPS-style segmentation for regions. Pure Python, deterministic, zero I/O, sitting behind ports.

As I mentioned, I made this to be a tool to help people find and get employed in this tough job market. Unfortunately, I knew this could only do so much which is why I tried to expand on that very idea!

records.title: Show HN: Gretel – Topic specific feeds built from YouTube recommendations
records.author: Ezap2
records.storyText:
One of the annoying things about YouTube is that it is really good at catching my attention, but I have little control over what kind of feed it can show me, so it becomes distracting instead. I don't want to hide recommendations entirely though, I just don't want all my interests mixed into one feed.

So I wondered if I could have separate YouTube profiles for different interests, but make creating one as simple as picking a few topics instead of having to create or connect another Google account.

So I built Gretel, a desktop app. It uses YT.js to access YouTube, and it runs locally so the requests come from my own machine rather than a server.

I create profiles, each with their own topics. Gretel then searches YouTube for the topics, collects candidate videos, and creates an embedding that is used to filter videos later on.

From the candidate videos, Gretel fetches related videos and continuously expands outward while filtering unrelated videos. This creates the base feed. After that, as I watch videos, the topic embeddings are continuously updated, and at the same time Gretel persists the YouTube sessions so the recommendations adapt as well.

I have been working on Gretel on and off for a while. It's beta: usable but still rough. I am curious if, after using a profile for a while, the feed actually starts converging toward what you wanted. Bug reports and contributions are welcome too.

You can sign in with Google to use the included embedding credits, or bring your own OpenRouter key. Other providers and local embedding models are coming.

records.title: Show HN: Delegator – Stop juggling coding-agent sessions
records.author: mattm
records.storyText:
I wanted to share Delegator with the HN community. delegator gives you a personal inbox to manage your tasks that is completely local to your machine.

Backstory: Like everyone else, I've been experimenting with different AI-assisted development workflows. I realized I was having difficulty with all the context switching between tasks. Asking agents to develop code ends up taking about 5-10 minutes usually for well-scoped tasks. At the beginning I would read the AI output as it went along and sometimes interrupt to guide it. But as LLMs have gotten better, there's less need to do that. So I would spin up another task during the latency and then another. (I wrote a little bit about this previously here https://mattmccormick.ca/we-re-all-managers-now-my-journey-i... )

Jumping back and forth between terminals with the Agent being at different stages was mentally taxing. I experimented with some different options and ended up realizing that to avoid the drain of context-switching, what I really needed was a queue.

Delegator works by putting all scoped tasks through the system. It stops when the ready queue has reached your configured limit. This is to prevent too much work from piling up waiting for review. It also presents the work from getting too far ahead in case any issues are found as part of development.

I also realized that for most tasks, agents can be treated as a background process. You pass in the work to the process. It processes it and then gives you an output to review. All changes are made in git worktrees for safety.

Who's it for? Delegator is for engineers who still want to understand the code and changes. It's not for vibe-coding or exploratory work. Don't get me wrong, I'll still spin up an agent session for brainstorming design options. But once I'm aligned on a direction, I'll then ask the agent to break down the work into "dg tickets". Since Delegator is a local program, agents can interact with it quickly and seamlessly.

Right now it's just CLI based but I'm looking to expand this into a GUI/Desktop App so I would be interested in any feedback you have. Let me know if you have any questions and I'll respond. The code is source available so you can check it out at https://github.com/alcubie/delegator if you want to check anything.

records.title: Show HN: Datapuddle, a native macOS DuckDB client that doesn't page results
records.author: harisamin
records.storyText:
I've been using DuckDB as a swiss army knife for a while now.

I have a soft spot for pretty/polished macOS apps. It bugged me there wasn't one for DuckDB. TablePlus is my favorite multi-db client, I'm in it daily, but the DuckDB support is thin.

The other thing was paging. Every client gives you the first N rows and a "load more" button. I didn't want that. DuckDB is the only place on my local machine where I actually am dealing, slicing/dicing, and perusing large datasets.

So I built Datapuddle to fully embrace DuckDB for in a macOS friendly way :)

The grid:

- Whole result is in it. Not the first page. Rows never become objects, cells get read out of DuckDB's columnar chunks at draw time and drawn with Core Text. Memory is flat at 40 rows or 41 million. Row 41,000,000 costs what row 40 costs.

- Numbers, on 20M rows x 30 cols out of an 11GB file: 119 fps average on a sustained fling, min-instantaneous 52-60, 2.8GB resident, jump to last row under a third of a millisecond.

- I tested this thoroughly on my M1 Max MacBook Pro with 64 GB RAM

Everything else:

- Column headers draw their own distribution, null share, distinct count.

- Query plans as a waterfall, or a tree, or raw JSON.

- History is local SQLite with FTS, so you can dig up last week's query from a fragment.

- Completion knows your schema. Connections saved, secrets in the Keychain.

- Extensions are statically linked, so DuckDB's reach is the app's: Parquet, CSV, JSON, .duckdb, local or on S3. Postgres tables attach alongside, so you can join across them. Nothing downloads at runtime.

- Speaks Quack, so you can point it at your own DuckDB server. Want an extension I didn't bundle? spatial, say. Load it there, query through it. Costs about 2x to pull the result across, then it's identical.

- No Electron. No webviews. No bundled Chromium to draw a table.

- Sends nothing anywhere. There's a build check that fails if anything linked in can open a socket.

$39.99 once, not a subscription, 7 day trial first. Apple Silicon, macOS 14+. Swift 6, AppKit. Around 3-4 months of work.

On AI, because someone always asks: couple of decades as an engineer, shipped native apps long before any of this existed. I used Claude throughout. Two places it really earned its keep: getting DuckDB and the extension set statically bundled and actually behaving, and the buffered Core Text grid. The rules were mine and enforcing them was most of the work. No DuckDB call on the main thread. Result rows never become objects. AppKit for anything that renders your data.

App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6811235967

Happy to go into any of it.

Some results:

- Holding Longest Road and Largest Army at the end wins 99% of games; holding neither wins 2%.

- Each pip of opening production over your opponent is worth about 4 points of win rate.

- The biggest improvement was patience: saving cards for the next city instead of spending them on roads and dev cards (62% vs. the original strategy).

- Several "obvious" ideas did nothing or hurt: valuing ports highly (44.8%), an endgame mode, a deeper search.

The README lists every experiment, including the rejected ones, with game counts and 95% intervals.

records.title: Show HN: I remade Mortyr's 2093-1944 engine using my own programming language
records.author: Panzerschrek
records.storyText:
Hello, HN!

Today I want to show my recent project called PanzerMortyr. It's a reimplementation of the engine of the game Mortyr 2093-1944 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortyr).

The most interesting thing about it is that it's written in my own programming language named Ü, which I developed previously and continue developing. See https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45769161, https://github.com/Panzerschrek/U-00DC-Sprache/.

I have spend almost a year developing PanzerMortyr. It took a lot of time, since I needed reverse-engineering data formats and logic of the original game and reimplementing it from scratch. No ready to use game engine was used, almost anything, what is needed, was written in Ü.

All code is written and designed by hand. No LLM or something similar was involved at all.

This project of mine has proven, that Ü is a mature language suitable for developing of complex programs. PanzerMortyr has more than 70000 lines of code, which includes data loading code, game logic, rendering (using OpenGL and a hand-written software rasterizer), audio code, etc. Thanks to Ü design preventing memory safety issues and minimizing other bugs without sacrificing performance I have achieved great performance without spending much time debugging and fixing bugs in such a huge codebase.

A video demonstrating actual gameplay and graphics (with software rendering): https://youtu.be/NepOPAPDvwA

An article describing some aspects of PanzerMortyr's development in details: https://gist.github.com/Panzerschrek/4e61056f6ce8055ab5fc1d5...

records.title: Show HN: Puppet Master – Manage coding agents at scale
records.author: chrismoos
records.storyText:
As I started to use `claude` and `codex` more it became too hard to manage all the sessions across all my tmux panes and sessions, so I built Puppet Master.

I see now there is quite a lot out there now for managing agents to write software, but

a) I started working on this before a lot of them, and b) there are things in Puppet Master that just don't exist all in one product.

For me I'd say the highlights are:

1) Web instead of terminal -- it's just a richer interface

2) iOS app so I can keep working on things from anywhere

3) Local + Remote workers (heterogeneous fleet), I work on things that are cross-platform and PM lets agents spawn across the fleet depending on workload needs.

4) Connections - first-class support for integrating MCP and REST API (ala OpenAPI definitions) into your agents. This goes above and beyond what a single harness can do via i.e an MCP integration. PM imports it (scoped to a bucket/project) and associates it to a policy. It lives between the agent and the remote MCP/API and enforces a policy. My normal flow is give full read access to agents and any APIs that do writes, approval needed. PM has native approval UI on web AND mobile so you can give real agency to your agents without being too permissive.

5) Code review interface is nice, 1-1 discussions on comment threads in the review, pretty responsive.

6) Forwards/artifacts allow agents to share static artifacts/html/etc,. OR serve up any dev server. This is proxied so even things on remote workers "just work" and you can access them, securely.

GitHub: https://github.com/chrismoos/puppet-master

records.title: Show HN: AgentOS – Run your coding agents from your phone, self-hosted
records.author: saadn92
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I posted AgentOS here a few months ago. Back then, it was pretty amazing to see what these agents can do and I'm improved it a lot since then.

The biggest change is that it's built for my phone now. I start work at my desk, walk away, and check on it or answer an agent from my phone over Tailscale. Chat sessions run in their own process, so restarting the server doesn't kill a turn that's halfway done.

It also runs tasks now. You give it a prompt, it makes a git worktree, the agent works there and opens a PR, and I review it later. Each workspace can have an orchestrator that starts tasks, reviews the PRs and merges the ones that pass CI and a review of that exact commit. Anything risky comes to me as an ask that needs Face ID to approve.

It supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Aider, Cursor CLI, Amp and Pi. It's still free and all self-hosted.

npm install -g @saadnvd1/agent-os

https://github.com/saadnvd1/agent-os

I'd love feedback and as I'm sure there will be issues, please share them! Also, if you want to build your own, just fork it. It's all free.

records.title: Show HN: Free native macOS Photoshop Clone with integrated AI harness
records.author: terhechte
records.storyText:
Hey all!

For the past months I've been vibe-coding a free Photoshop editor for macOS (Native using Swift and a bit of Rust). It has many features that I've always wanted in such an editor (but was unwilling to pay the Adobe tax).

I did try open source solutions such as Gimp but they never worked for me. In terms of features I'm not gonna list all, but I'm very happy it has:

- A proper canvas where text and vectors keep their quality when zooming in - Layers (vectors, text, pixels, color adjustment, effects, reference layers, mask layers, layer groups and so on) - Many effects (including unusual things like dithering or NTSC) - All the tools you'd expect (brush, paint, repair, etc) For some of these tools it uses local models - Selection operations via local models (e.g. select all red cars) - Import / Export PSD, SVG and many others. - Support for tracing images to vectors, text to beziers, bezier editing, etc.

Most importantly (I think), it has a optional AI integration via a agent harness which lets a model remote-control the app for you to build a document out of layers & effects & brushes etc. This is really powerful because in comparison to typical genai flows this allows you to make changes, hide things and easily scale them up (if most elements are vectors). There's also support for genai operations (e.g. if you want to embed a genai generated SVG or image as a new layer).

Would love to get feedback:

https://pixellect.app/

records.title: Show HN: Deploylist – StumbleUpon feed for upvoted web projects on HN and Reddit
records.author: henry-xli
records.storyText:
I’ve seen indie development take off over the past few years, but many attempts to capture this creativity and revive the StumbleUpon concept have fallen short, mostly due to having lackluster entries. My website allows forums to act as a tried-and-true quality filtering system to show you the best of the online development scene.

This site runs an automatic ingestion every 3 days, selecting the most-upvoted posts across all the linked subreddits and Hacker News over the past week and month (feel free to suggest more good sources of web projects), that center around a standalone project hosted on a non-major site (so not Github, App Store, Steam, etc). In this way, projects can be viewed quickly and easily within the browser. Websites with embedding issues are still ranked on the leaderboard, but aren’t shown in the live view. Ideally, this website stirs your creativity, serves a somewhat-accurate snapshot of the web development scene, and shows that the internet can still be fun to explore.

Try the live feed yourself: deploylist.com

records.title: Show HN: TOD,a universal Decision model based on Task Oriented Design
records.author: suriyaG
records.storyText:
Hi HN, we built TOD, a model and API for jevlike LLM pipelines.

we have people using it for, routing a ticket, classifying intent, deciding whether something is urgent, or rating severity.

Architecture - 12B Gemma fine-tuned to score options. since it is gemma based it has multimodality built in - When there are >120 labels, we have a 150M retriever that narrows them to a shortlist (recall@16 is 0.9–1.0 on our evals), and the 12B model scores that shortlist. - Context goes up to 49k tokens, with up to 8 images per request.

we have open sourced it,

model: https://huggingface.co/parsecai/tod API: https://parseclab.ai/tod

We are working on getting the RL environments to finetune for custom use cases.

would love to hear your opinions on this.
